rationale: Defines 'major ICT-related incident', one of the triggers that DORA 6(5) names; the answer can name the trigger without the definition, and the need does not use the term.
The duty to have 'a sound, comprehensive and well-documented ICT risk management framework': it is what gets reviewed, but it states neither the frequency nor the triggers.

The framework 'shall be documented and reviewed at least once a year' and 'upon the occurrence of major ICT-related incidents, and following supervisory instructions or conclusions derived from relevant digital operational resilience testing or audit processes': the cycle and the triggers asked for.
Same 'at least yearly' wording, but its object is 'the risk scenarios impacting them', not the ICT risk management framework: it applies to the bank and still answers neither question.

It requires entities to 'regularly review their ICT business continuity policy and ICT response and recovery plans', a duty the lead-in places 'As part of their comprehensive ICT risk management': it reviews a part of the framework, not the framework, and states neither a frequency nor an extra trigger for the framework review, so it is not 3 or 2. It is a different obligation rather than the same rule in a parallel regime, so the twin rule does not force a 0, and since a calendar for the framework can reasonably draw on the reviews of its parts it is not 'definitely not relevant' (section 2, scope check) but useful context a correct answer can leave out: grade 1.

It requires 'post ICT-related incident reviews after a major ICT-related incident disrupts their core activities', analysing 'the causes of disruption': this reviews the incident, not the framework, so the answer on the framework's cycle and triggers is correct and complete without it (not 2). Because it fires on a major ICT-related incident and its output is 'required improvements to the ICT operations or within the ICT business continuity policy referred to in Article 11', a part of the ICT risk management, it is not 'definitely not relevant' as section 2 requires for a 0, but useful context a correct answer can leave out: grade 1.
A mandate for standards on 'the content and format of the report on the review of the ICT risk management framework': it does not fix the frequency or the triggers asked for.

The simplified framework is 'reviewed periodically and upon the occurrence of major ICT-related incidents', but it is the framework 'referred to in paragraph 1, second subparagraph, point (a)', and 16(1) lists small and non-interconnected investment firms, exempted payment, e-money and credit institutions and small IORPs: a mid-sized bank is none of them.
The lead-in 'this Regulation applies to the following entities:' turns point (b) into the scope rule; without it point (b) is a bare list item.
'payment institutions, including payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366': the exempt small payment business is covered by DORA.

'electronic money institutions, including electronic money institutions exempted pursuant to Directive 2009/110/EC' has the same construction but reaches e-money institutions; the need states an exemption for small payment institutions.
Entities in points (a) to (t) 'shall collectively be referred to as financial entities': a name the answer does not need.

The exclusions ('This Regulation does not apply to:') to which paragraph 1 is subject; its points name fund managers, certain insurers, small IORPs, persons exempted under the investment-services directive, small insurance intermediaries and post office giro institutions, none of which the facts make the business, so it cannot change the answer.

Point (d) takes out of DORA only 'natural or legal persons exempted pursuant to Articles 2 and 3 of Directive 2014/65/EU', an investment-services exemption, while the need states a business under the exemption for small payment institutions, so the facts rule this exclusion out. Under the exceptions rule ('1 when the facts of the need rule them out') it is a 1, not a hard negative: it is an exclusion from the very scope the need asks about, and useful contrast because it is the case where an exemption does keep a person outside DORA, which is the founder's assumption.

The option lets Member States exclude only 'entities referred to in Article 2(5), points (4) to (23), of Directive 2013/36/EU', and DORA:16.1 lists 'institutions exempted pursuant to Directive 2013/36/EU' apart from 'payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366', so the facts of the need rule this derogation out. Under the exceptions rule ('1 when the facts of the need rule them out') it is a 1 rather than a 0: a scope derogation the answer checks and sets aside, useful context for a founder who relies on a national exemption, which a correct and complete answer can leave out.
Defines 'payment institution' by reference to Directive (EU) 2015/2366; DORA 2(1)(b) names the exempted ones expressly, so the answer does not depend on this definition.

The derogation applies on the stated facts ('Articles 5 to 15 of this Regulation shall not apply to ... payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366'), but it presupposes that the business is within DORA and only lightens its ICT risk management regime, so it cannot change the answer to whether the business is covered 'at all', and the exceptions rule gives 2 only to a derogation that 'would change the answer'. The extent of the obligations is not asked, so this is useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out (grade 1), not a node without which the answer would be wrong or incomplete.
Names the competent authority 'for payment institutions, including payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366': it confirms coverage, but the answer stands on Article 2.
A 'payment institution' is one 'granted authorisation in accordance with Article 11': it explains why DORA has to name exempted payment institutions separately, but the answer can leave it out.

Member States may exempt persons providing payment services 'from the application of all or part of the procedure and conditions': it is the exemption the founder uses, and the need already describes it in those terms, so the mapping is obvious.
Exempted persons 'shall be treated as payment institutions': it supports the reading of DORA's 'payment institutions exempted', which DORA 2(1)(b) states by itself.
The exemption of persons 'providing only the payment service as referred to in point (8) of Annex I' is the account-information exemption, not the small payment institution exemption the need states.
Custody and administration is 'the safekeeping or controlling, on behalf of clients, of crypto-assets': the need already says 'keeps its customers' tokens in custody', so the mapping is obvious.
The 'register of positions' opened in the name of each client: background to the statement, not the frequency or the request.

'A summary of the custody policy shall be made available to clients at their request in an electronic format': it applies to custodians, but it concerns the custody policy, not a statement of the crypto-assets held.

Custodians 'shall provide their clients, at least once every three months and at the request of the client concerned, with a statement of position of the crypto-assets recorded in the name of those clients'.
Information 'about operations on crypto-assets that require a response from those clients': other client reporting, which a correct answer can leave out.

'periodic statements ... of the portfolio management activities carried out on their behalf' bind providers 'providing portfolio management'; even if the exchange also managed portfolios, that statement is about the activities, not the crypto-assets it holds in custody.

'The periodic statement referred to in the first subparagraph ... shall be provided every three months': the same figure for the portfolio-management statement, not for the custody statement asked for.

'A person shall not provide crypto-asset services, within the Union, unless' authorised: 61(1) disapplies 'the requirement for authorisation under Article 59', so the answer needs the rule it refers to.

The point only names the route the firm lacks ('authorised as crypto-asset service provider in accordance with Article 63'), which the need already presupposes ('without an EU authorisation'), and the exclusive-initiative exemption (MiCA Art. 61(1)) itself names the Article 59 authorisation requirement it disapplies, so neither question is answered wrongly or incompletely without this point. It is not a definition, condition, exception or lead-in, and under the whole-article reference rule a cross-reference 'never adds qrels by itself': useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out, grade 1.

The firm is 'a person who is not a crypto-asset service provider' and must not 'issue marketing communications ... suggesting that it is a crypto-asset service provider', but this bites only on email content the need does not give, and even then it would not change the answer: Art. 61.2 ('shall not entitle a third-country firm to market new types of crypto-assets or crypto-asset services') and 61.1 sub 2 (solicitation ends the client's own exclusive initiative) already say no. Under section 2 it is useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out, so grade 1, not a condition that changes the answer (2).
Freedom to 'provide crypto-asset services throughout the Union' belongs to authorised crypto-asset service providers; the need states that the firm has no MiCA authorisation.
Where a client 'initiates at its own exclusive initiative' the service of a third-country firm, 'the requirement for authorisation under Article 59 shall not apply': the answer to the first question.

A firm that 'solicits clients or prospective clients in the Union, regardless of the means of communication used for the solicitation, promotion or advertising' does not serve at the client's own initiative: a condition that changes both answers.
Solicitation counts 'notwithstanding any contractual clause or disclaimer': it reinforces the condition without changing the answer.
The client's own exclusive initiative does 'not entitle a third-country firm to market new types of crypto-assets or crypto-asset services to that client': the answer to the email question.
A mandate for guidelines on 'the situations in which a third-country firm is deemed to solicit clients': Article 61 itself answers both questions, so it does not fix the element asked for.

The notification by 'A crypto-asset service provider that intends to provide crypto-asset services in more than one Member State' presupposes an authorised provider with a home Member State; the firm has no MiCA authorisation.
Defines 'crypto-asset service provider': the need's 'crypto exchange authorised under MiCA' maps to it obviously; it says nothing about transfer data.
Transfer services move crypto-assets 'from one distributed ledger address or account to another': it names the activity, not the data that must accompany it.
Procedures 'to comply with the provisions of national law transposing Directive (EU) 2015/849': it points to anti-money-laundering law, but states no data that must travel with a transfer.
Transfer service providers 'shall conclude an agreement with their clients': the only MiCA duty on transfer services, about the client agreement, not the transfer data.
'the identity of the parties to the agreement' is a term of the client agreement under 82(1), not information that must accompany each transfer; no reading of the facts makes it so.

Under Article 82 ('Providing transfer services for crypto-assets on behalf of clients') and the lead-in of paragraph 1 on the agreement the provider concludes with its clients, the node only makes 'a description of the modalities of the transfer service provided' a term of that agreement. It states no information about the sender or the recipient that must accompany a transfer, and it is not a definition, condition or exception that could change that answer, so it fails grades 3 and 2; sharing the topic of transfers is not the 'useful context' of grade 1. Scope check: the actor of the lead-in can be the exchange in the need, and no unstated fact turns a term of the client agreement into information accompanying each transfer, so the node is definitely not relevant and takes grade 0 (section 2, hard negatives and the scope check).
Guidelines on transfer 'procedures and policies, including the rights of clients': it does not say that the data asked for are fixed there.

The node says PSD2 'Articles 28, 29 and 30 shall be without prejudice to the obligation of competent authorities ... to supervise or monitor the compliance' with Directive (EU) 2015/849 and Regulation (EU) 2015/847. It binds supervisors, imposes nothing on the exchange and states no information about the sender or the recipient. Its mention of 'Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2015/847' is cited for that supervisory duty and only marks where to look, since 'A cross-reference never adds qrels by itself' (section 2, references to whole articles). Scope check: even if the exchange also came within those PSD2 articles, the node would still state nothing that must accompany a transfer, so it is definitely not relevant and takes grade 0 (hard negatives and the scope check).

Under 45(1) the provider gives its own user 'a specification of the information or unique identifier to be provided by the payment service user': information from provider to user before a payment, not data that travel with a transfer, whatever the asset.
Under 57(1) the payer's provider gives the payer, after the debit, 'information relating to the payee': information returned to the payer, not data that travel with a transfer.
DORA applies to 'crypto-asset service providers as authorised under' MiCA: context, since the need asks what the policy must contain under the crypto rules.
Sets the DORA 'comprehensive ICT business continuity policy' within the ICT risk management framework: part of the referred Article 11, context for the MiCA policy.
DORA's own aims for the ICT business continuity policy ('aiming to:'); the need asks what the policy must achieve under the crypto rules, which MiCA states.

The node requires entities to 'implement associated ICT response and recovery plans' and, for non-microenterprises, 'independent internal audit reviews', but the crypto rule quoted in the record already names this plan ('ICT response and recovery plans set up pursuant to Articles 11 and 12') together with its aims, so under the whole-article reference rule ('marks where to look, not what is relevant') the answer is neither wrong nor incomplete without this node. The audit requirement concerns the plans themselves, not what the policy must contain or aim at, so the node is useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out: grade 1.

'put in place, maintain and periodically test appropriate ICT business continuity plans' sets up and tests the plan, but the need asks only which plans the policy must include and what it must aim at, and the crypto rule names 'ICT business continuity plans' itself. Under the whole-article reference rule a correct and complete answer can leave this node out, so it is useful context: grade 1.
A business impact analysis 'as part of the overall business continuity policy': a DORA element of the policy, not one the crypto rules name; context.
Testing the plans 'at least yearly': the plans named by MiCA must be tested, but the need does not ask how often; context.

The lead-in 'For the purpose of ensuring the restoration of ICT systems and data with minimum downtime, limited disruption and loss ... shall develop and document:' belongs to the referred Article 12 and echoes the recovery aim, but no part of Article 12 is needed to say which plans the policy must include or what it must aim at. The clause 'ambiguous when it cannot be told which part is needed' therefore does not arise, and the node is useful context: grade 1.

'restoration and recovery procedures and methods' are procedures behind recovery, not one of the plans the crypto rule requires the policy to include (it names only 'ICT business continuity plans' and 'ICT response and recovery plans'), and the answer is complete without them. Under the whole-article reference rule this is useful context, grade 1, and it is not ambiguous because the answer needs no part of Article 12.
Backup systems, and periodic testing of backup and restoration procedures: part of the referred Article 12, not needed to say which plans the policy includes.

Business continuity plans under the simplified framework of the entities listed in 16(1), which names small investment firms, exempted payment, e-money and credit institutions and small IORPs, not a crypto-asset service provider.
Defines 'crypto-asset service provider': the need's 'crypto exchange authorised under MiCA' maps to it obviously.

The same continuity wording, but 'Issuers of asset-referenced tokens shall establish a business continuity policy': the need is about a crypto exchange's policy, and nothing says it issues such tokens.
The general duty to 'ensure continuity and regularity in the performance of their crypto-asset services': the policy's content is stated in the second subparagraph.

Providers 'shall establish a business continuity policy, which shall include ICT business continuity plans as well as ICT response and recovery plans set up pursuant to Articles 11 and 12' of DORA 'that aim to ensure ... the preservation of essential data and functions and the maintenance of crypto-asset services' or their timely recovery.

Providers 'operating a trading platform' must keep trading systems 'subject to effective business continuity arrangements': a crypto exchange may operate one, so it is potentially useful context, but it is a separate duty from the policy.

Ten business days apply to 'a request for a refund'; 77(1) limits those requests to 'the refund referred to in Article 76 of an authorised payment transaction', and under 64(1) a transaction is authorised 'only if the payer has given consent': a second charge of the same card payment had no consent.
Procedures for complaints 'to the competent authorities' about alleged infringements: the need states that she complained to her provider, and this node sets no reply deadline for the provider.
Providers must have 'adequate and effective complaint resolution procedures': context, no deadline.
Reply 'at the latest within 15 business days of receipt of the complaint'; 'In exceptional situations' beyond the provider's control, a holding reply, and the final reply within 35 business days.
Member States may keep or introduce rules 'more advantageous to the payment service user': a derogation that can shorten the deadline, and the need names no Member State.

The node puts a duty on the same provider for the same kind of dispute ('shall inform the payment service user about at least one ADR entity which is competent to deal with disputes concerning the rights and obligations arising under Titles III and IV'). The need does not say whether the reply comes late or leaves her unsatisfied, and on a reasonable reading of those open facts this is potentially useful context, so the scope check rules out a 0, which is kept for 'definitely not relevant', never 'probably not relevant'. It states no reply deadline and no case in which the reply may take longer, so a correct and complete answer can leave it out: grade 1, not 2.
Member States must establish 'ADR procedures for the settlement of disputes': a different channel, with no deadline for the provider's reply.

A direct debit is 'initiated by the payee on the basis of the consent given by the payer to the payee': it confirms that the signed form is consent, but the need already uses the term in its legal sense.
A transaction 'is considered to be authorised only if the payer has given consent': the signed mandate is that consent, so the debit is authorised; the need makes this evident, context.
Consent 'may also be given via the payee': supports that signing the gym's form is consent; context.

Rectification of 'an unauthorised or incorrectly executed payment transaction' within 13 months: she signed a mandate that 'did not state a fixed amount', so the larger debit is within her consent (64(1), 64(2)) and was executed as ordered.
The next-business-day refund applies 'in the case of an unauthorised payment transaction'; the debit was authorised by the signed mandate, which fixed no amount.

'a payer is entitled to a refund ... of an authorised payment transaction which was initiated by or through a payee ... if both of the following conditions are met': the right exists despite the signed mandate.

Read with the Article 76(1) lead-in ('if both of the following conditions are met'), 'the authorisation did not specify the exact amount of the payment transaction when the authorisation was made' is one of two cumulative conditions of the refund right. The right itself ('a payer is entitled to a refund ... of an authorised payment transaction') is stated in the lead-in; section 2 grades a condition 2 when it 'can apply to the need and would change the answer', and here the need's form 'did not state a fixed amount' and without this condition there is no refund. The need asks whether she can get the money back, not for a list of conditions, so the list clause does not raise a single condition to 3.

Read with the same lead-in ('if both of the following conditions are met'), 'the amount of the payment transaction exceeded the amount the payer could reasonably have expected taking into account the previous spending pattern' is the second cumulative condition of the refund right, not the right itself. It can apply to the need ('a much larger monthly amount than usual') and would change the answer if it were not met, so section 2 grades it 2 ('an exception, condition or derogation that can change the answer'); the need asks a yes or no question about the right, not for the list of conditions, so the list clause does not make it a 3.
The payer bears 'the burden of proving such conditions are met' on request: practical detail.
The refund is 'the full amount': detail of the refund, not whether she gets it.

The node answers the question directly: 'the payer has an unconditional right to a refund within the time limits laid down in Article 77'. But it applies only 'for direct debits as referred to in Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 260/2012', and the need does not state the currency or the scheme of the debit. That fact could reasonably hold for a gym debit, but the need does not establish it. Under section 2 ('Applicability that depends on unstated facts'), 'The need does not exclude it' never establishes that a node applies, so this is a 2, not a 3. A missing fact alone does not make the node ambiguous.
A framework contract may provide that 'the payer has no right to a refund where': the need does not say where she gave consent, so the exception can apply and would change the answer.
Exception condition: consent given 'directly to the payment service provider'; open on the facts.
Exception condition: information on the future transaction provided 'for at least 4 weeks before the due date'; open on the facts.
For direct debits 'in currencies other than euro', Member States may offer more favourable rights: context.
The payer 'can request the refund ... for a period of 8 weeks from the date on which the funds were debited': about six weeks later, she still can.
Within 10 business days the provider refunds or justifies a refusal: how the bank responds, which the need no longer asks; context.
The right to refuse 'shall not apply' to the unconditional refund of 76(1) fourth subparagraph: it confirms that branch, which 76(1) already states as 'unconditional'; context.
'ICT third-party service provider' means 'an undertaking providing ICT services': the vendor running the core banking platform obviously is one, and no other category is plausible.
Defines 'ICT services'; the core banking platform obviously is one; not needed for the answer.

The lead-in 'Financial entities shall ensure that contractual arrangements on the use of ICT services may be terminated in any of the following circumstances:' turns points (a) to (d) into termination situations.
Situation: 'significant breach by the ICT third-party service provider of applicable laws, regulations or contractual terms'.
Situation: circumstances found in monitoring 'deemed capable of altering the performance of the functions provided through the contractual arrangement', including material changes.
Situation: the provider's 'evidenced weaknesses pertaining to its overall ICT risk management'.
Situation: 'where the competent authority can no longer effectively supervise the financial entity' because of the arrangement.
Exit strategies must take into account 'the termination of contractual arrangements ... under any of the circumstances listed in paragraph 7': it refers back to the answer; context.
Lead-in of the minimum contract content ('shall include at least the following elements:'); only point (h) concerns termination, and it is context, so the lead-in is too.

Access, recovery and return of data 'in the event of the termination of the contractual arrangements': what happens on termination, not when; context for someone reviewing the right to end the contract.
The contract must include 'termination rights and related minimum notice periods': it requires termination rights but names no situation; context.

The Lead Overseer assesses a critical provider's portability mechanisms 'which ensure an effective exercise of termination rights by the financial entities': the need does not say whether the vendor is critical; if it is, this is useful context, never the answer.

The node only obliges the Lead Overseer to 'inform the critical ICT third-party service provider of the consequences of such opposition, including the possibility' that authorities require termination, so even if the vendor were critical it would not itself state a situation in which the bank must be able to end the contract, and a complete answer can leave it out (grade 1, section 2). The need leaves open whether the vendor is critical, so the scope check rules out a 0 and makes it potentially useful context; no reading raises it above 1, so its grade is settled and it is not ambiguous.

Unlike a notice, this is the operative power: competent authorities 'may require financial entities to terminate, in part or completely, the relevant contractual arrangements concluded with the critical ICT third-party service providers', which adds a situation in which the bank must be able to end the contract only if the vendor is critical and only if the need's 'must be able to end' covers termination ordered by an authority, not just the circumstances the contract itself must allow. The need settles neither the vendor's status nor that reading, so the grade (1, or 2 or more) depends on interpretation and its applicability cannot be settled: ambiguous under the scope check and section 4, with grade 1 recorded.

Outsourcing agreements must give 'crypto-asset service providers the right to terminate': under 73(1) this binds crypto-asset service providers that outsource, and the need is about a bank's core banking contract.

A periodic penalty payment that the Lead Overseer imposes 'to compel the critical ICT third-party service provider': under 35(1) these powers are 'in respect of the critical ICT third-party service providers', not an insurer fined by its national supervisor.

'up to 1 % of the average daily worldwide turnover of the critical ICT third-party service provider': a ceiling of the Lead Overseer's powers over critical providers (35(1)), not a fine on an insurer by its national supervisor.
The authority 'for insurance and reinsurance undertakings' is the one designated under Directive 2009/138/EC: it identifies the national supervisor, which the need already names; context.
Competent authorities 'shall have all supervisory, investigatory and sanctioning powers necessary': the power exists, but no amount.

'Member States shall lay down rules establishing appropriate administrative penalties and remedial measures': it states where the maximum is fixed (national law); without it an answer could take a DORA figure that does not apply.
Penalties must be 'effective, proportionate and dissuasive': a standard, not an amount.
The lead-in by which authorities get 'the power to apply at least the following administrative penalties or remedial measures': it turns point (c) into a power.
'adopt any type of measure, including of pecuniary nature': the basis for a fine, stated without any amount; needed for a complete answer.
Criteria for 'the type and level' of a penalty: how a fine is sized within national law, not its maximum.

Article 52(1) lets Member States 'decide not to lay down rules for administrative penalties or remedial measures for breaches that are subject to criminal penalties'. That decides whether a supervisory fine exists at all, not how high it can go, and the need assumes that 'the company's national supervisor fined it', so the facts of the need rule the derogation out. Under section 2 (exceptions, conditions and derogations: '1 when the facts of the need rule them out') it is useful context on criminal exposure for the board briefing, so it is a 1, not a 2 and not a 0.
'maximum administrative fines of at least' for legal persons apply to the MiCA infringements listed in 111(1); an insurer's shortfall under DORA is not one of them.
'3 % of the average daily turnover' is the amount of periodic penalty payments that EBA imposes under 132(1); nothing in the need involves EBA or MiCA.
Penalties for 'infringements of the national law transposing this Directive', the payment services directive; the need is about an insurer falling short of DORA.

Quotes 'reporting of major ICT-related incidents and notifying, on a voluntary basis, significant cyber threats to the competent authorities'. Read with the lead-ins of Article 1 ('this Regulation lays down uniform requirements ... requirements applicable to financial entities in relation to:'), it describes the subject matter of the Regulation and restates the very contrast the need turns on, but it lays down no rule: the operative provision, with its addressee and condition, is 19(2). Corroboration that a correct and complete answer can leave out: 1.

''ICT-related incident' means a single event or a series of linked events unplanned by the financial entity that compromises the security of the network and information systems, and have an adverse impact on the availability, authenticity, integrity or confidentiality of data, or on the services provided by the financial entity'. It confirms that a detected threat that has affected no system or service is not an ICT-related incident, so 19(1) is not engaged. The need itself states that no incident has happened and no system or service has been affected, so the answer does not depend on reading this definition: context, 1.

''major ICT-related incident' means an ICT-related incident that has a high adverse impact on the network and information systems that support critical or important functions'. It fixes the object of the mandatory duty the lead has in mind (19(1)); with no incident at all the threshold never comes into play. Context that explains why the lead's analogy fails, not needed for the answer: 1.

The definition ('a cyber threat the technical characteristics of which indicate that it could have the potential to result in a major ICT-related incident') only bounds which threats the bank may notify 'on a voluntary basis' under Article 19(2), so the answer that there is no duty to report the threat to the supervisor holds whether or not the 'serious' threat meets it, and the line between threat and incident is already drawn by the stated facts ('No incident has happened'). Under the definitions rule (2 only if, without it, the need could reasonably be answered wrongly or incompletely) and the rule that a condition is 2 only when it would change the answer, it is useful context: 1.

'Financial entities shall record all ICT-related incidents and significant cyber threats.' A duty DORA does attach to significant threats, but it is internal record-keeping, not reporting to the supervisor. Useful to show what DORA does require for a threat; a correct and complete answer to whether the bank must report it can leave it out: 1.

'Financial entities shall classify cyber threats as significant based on the criticality of the services at risk, ... number and/or relevance of clients or financial counterparts targeted and the geographical spread of the areas at risk.' It decides whether the threat is 'significant', and so whether the voluntary route of 19(2) is open; it does not change whether reporting is mandatory, which it is not under either classification. Context: 1.

Its object is 'major ICT-related incidents', that is an ICT-related incident that 'compromises the security of the network and information systems, and have an adverse impact on ... data, or on the services' (3(8), 3(10)), while the need states 'No incident has happened, and no system or service has been affected', so the scope check (actor matches under 2(1)(a) and 2(2), object excluded) leaves no reading under which it applies, and as the mandatory regime parallel to the voluntary one in the same article it is a 0 under the grade 0 and twins rules. It is not a 2: the lead's premise that major incidents must be reported is correct, and its extension to threats is corrected by 19(2) on its own ('may, on a voluntary basis, notify significant cyber threats'), so the answer is legally correct and complete without this node, which is not an exception, a referred provision or a definition the answer needs.

'Credit institutions classified as significant ... shall report major ICT-related incidents to the relevant national competent authority ..., which shall immediately transmit that report to the ECB' only routes the 19(1) duty, whose object, a major ICT-related incident (3(8), 3(10)), the stated facts rule out ('No incident has happened, and no system or service has been affected'), so the bank's unstated significance cannot make it apply and the scope check passes. It is the same wording as the voluntary threat route of 19(2), second subparagraph, with 'shall report major ICT-related incidents' in place of 'may, on a voluntary basis, notify significant cyber threats', so under the twins rule it is 0, not 1 as context.

'Financial entities may, on a voluntary basis, notify significant cyber threats to the relevant competent authority when they deem the threat to be of relevance to the financial system, service users or clients.' Read with the article heading ('... voluntary notification of significant cyber threats'), it answers the primary question directly: notifying a threat to the supervisor is an option, not a duty, open when the bank deems the threat relevant to the financial system, service users or clients. What makes it apply: the bank is a credit institution, hence a financial entity (2(1)(a), 2(2)), and the need describes a serious cyber threat with no incident, the situation of 19(2) and not of 19(1). Whether the threat reaches the 'significant' classification (3(13), 18(2)) only decides whether this voluntary route is open, not whether there is an obligation: 3.

'Credit institutions classified as significant, in accordance with Article 6(4) of Regulation (EU) No 1024/2013, may, on a voluntary basis, notify significant cyber threats to relevant national competent authority, designated in accordance with Article 4 of Directive 2013/36/EU, which shall immediately transmit the notification to the ECB.' It would answer directly, for the bank's own supervisory route (national authority to the ECB, 46(a)), but it applies only if the bank is a significant credit institution, a fact the need does not state and that could reasonably hold for a bank: 2.

'Member States may determine that those financial entities that on a voluntary basis notify in accordance with the first subparagraph may also transmit that notification to the CSIRTs ...' It presupposes and confirms the voluntary nature of the notification and adds an optional extra recipient chosen by national law; it does not change whether the bank must report. Context: 1.

'In the case of a significant cyber threat, financial entities shall, where applicable, inform their clients that are potentially affected of any appropriate protection measures which the latter may consider taking.' The only 'shall' in Article 19 triggered by a threat, but it runs to potentially affected clients, not to the supervisor. It does not answer whether the bank must report to its supervisor; useful context that a complete answer can leave out: 1.

Under the lead-in 'The ESAs ... shall develop: (a) common draft regulatory technical standards in order to:', point (iii) reads 'establish the content of the notification for significant cyber threats.' A mandate for Level 2 standards on the content of the voluntary notification; it does not fix whether notification is mandatory, the element asked. Context: 1.

'common draft implementing technical standards in order to establish the standard forms, templates and procedures for financial entities to report a major ICT-related incident and to notify a significant cyber threat.' Lexically close to the need and it mirrors the 'report' and 'notify' split of Article 19, but it is a mandate for templates and procedures and does not say whether notifying a threat is mandatory. Context: 1.

'Financial entities shall notify competent authorities of their participation in the information-sharing arrangements referred to in paragraph 1, upon validation of their membership, or, as applicable, of the cessation of their membership, once it takes effect.' Why it tempts: it is the only 'shall notify competent authorities' in the article on cyber threat information, so a query about a mandatory notification of a cyber threat can land on it. Why it is wrong: what must be notified is membership in, or exit from, an arrangement for exchanging threat information among financial entities (45(1), itself voluntary: 'may exchange'), never the threat. Whether the bank takes part in such an arrangement is not stated, but even if it does the node imposes no duty to report the threat: 0.

Under the lead-in 'By 17 January 2028, the Commission shall ... carry out a review ... The review shall include at least the following:', point (b) reads 'the voluntary nature of the notification of significant cyber threats referred to in Article 19;'. It confirms that the notification is voluntary and that this choice is under review, but it lays down no rule for the bank, and a later change would be another version of the law (out of scope). Corroborating context: 1.

'threat-led penetration testing (TLPT)' means a framework that ... delivers a controlled, bespoke, intelligence-led (red team) test of the financial entity's critical live production systems. The need already names TLPT under DORA and its 'in-house red team' maps plainly onto the testers of that test; the definition is not needed to decide whether internal staff may test. Context: 1.

'Financial entities, other than microenterprises, shall ensure that tests are undertaken by independent parties, whether internal or external. Where tests are undertaken by an internal tester, financial entities shall dedicate sufficient resources and ensure that conflicts of interest are avoided throughout the design and execution phases of the test.' General rule of the testing programme and twin of 27(2)(b), whose wording it repeats; a lexical retriever will take it for the TLPT rule, and an answer resting on it alone would say yes with no approval, no external threat intelligence, no rotation and no ban for significant credit institutions. Not a 0: 24(2) brings the tests of Article 26 into the programme it governs, so it also reaches the bank's TLPT. But for TLPT the specific rules of 26(8) and 27(2) decide the answer, and 27(2)(b) already carries its resources and conflict-of-interest condition under supervisory verification, so a correct and complete answer can leave it out: 1.

'The digital operational resilience testing programme referred to in Article 24 shall provide ... for the execution of appropriate tests, such as ... end-to-end testing and penetration testing.' Tempts because it names penetration testing among DORA's tests. Wrong on the stated facts: it lists the kinds of tests of the general programme, not TLPT (Article 26), and says nothing on who may perform a test; whether the bank's own staff may be its TLPT testers is settled by 26(8) and 27. No unstated fact would make it answer or change the answer: 0.

'... shall carry out at least every 3 years advanced testing by means of TLPT. Based on the risk profile of the financial entity ... the competent authority may, where necessary, request the financial entity to reduce or increase this frequency.' The TLPT duty itself, which the need takes as given ('has been required by its supervisor'); it says nothing about who may test. Context: 1.

'... the financial entity and the ICT third-party service provider may agree in writing that the ICT third-party service provider directly enters into contractual arrangements with an external tester, for the purpose of conducting ... a pooled TLPT'. Tempts because it is a TLPT rule naming an external tester. Wrong: it applies only where an ICT third-party service provider is in the TLPT scope (26(3)) and its participation is reasonably expected to harm its services to customers outside DORA or the confidentiality of their data, and then it lets that provider contract the tester of a pooled test. It neither allows nor forbids the bank's own staff as testers of the bank's TLPT, so even if a provider were in scope it would not answer or change the answer: 0.

'Financial entities shall contract testers for the purposes of undertaking TLPT in accordance with Article 27. When financial entities use internal testers for the purposes of undertaking TLPT, they shall contract external testers every three tests.' Answers directly: internal testers may be used, but not for every test, since external testers must be contracted every three tests, and the testers are governed by Article 27. Applies on the stated facts: a bank is a credit institution and so a financial entity (2(1)(a), 2(2)), it is required to perform TLPT, and it wants its in-house red team, that is internal testers, to perform 'the tests'. 3.

'Credit institutions that are classified as significant in accordance with Article 6(4) of Regulation (EU) No 1024/2013, shall only use external testers in accordance with Article 27(1), points (a) to (e).' Would answer no outright, but only if the bank is classified as significant, a fact the need does not state and that could reasonably hold for a bank selected for TLPT. Exception that can apply and would change the answer: 2. The criteria of significance are in Regulation 1024/2013, outside the corpus, but the answer needs only the classification, which is a fact about the bank.

'Member States may designate a single public authority in the financial sector to be responsible for TLPT-related matters in the financial sector at national level ...' Named by 27(2)(a) as a possible approver of internal testers; it says which authority that can be, while the approval condition itself is in 27(2)(a). Context: 1.

'In the absence of a designation ... a competent authority may delegate the exercise of some or all of the tasks referred to in this Article and Article 27 to another national authority in the financial sector.' Also named by 27(2)(a); it explains that the approval of internal testers may sit with a delegated authority. Context: 1.

'the criteria used for the purpose of the application of paragraph 8, second subparagraph;' (RTS mandate). Read literally, the RTS fix criteria for applying the rule that significant credit institutions use only external testers, which would place part of the exception in a Level 2 act outside the corpus (a 2). But that subparagraph already names its own criterion (classification under Article 6(4) of Regulation 1024/2013), and 'criteria used for ... the application' fits the identification of TLPT entities in the third subparagraph, which speaks of criteria and an assessment. The text cannot settle which subparagraph the mandate serves: best grade 1, ambiguous.

Read under its lead-in 'develop joint draft regulatory technical standards ... in order to specify further:', the node says the RTS fix 'the requirements and standards governing the use of internal testers'. That is exactly the use of in-house staff the need asks about. Those requirements are binding conditions on that use beyond the Level 1 text, and they can change whether the bank's red team may test, so the node is a 2 under the mandates rule ('2 when they say where the element asked for is fixed') and the grade-2 test for a condition that can change the answer. Rationale A says the conditions are fully fixed at Level 1, but the words 'specify further ... the requirements and standards governing the use of internal testers' contradict that, so a complete answer cannot drop this pointer as mere context (grade 1).

'Financial entities shall only use testers for the carrying out of TLPT, that:' Not the answer on internal versus external testers, but 27(2) applies these requirements to internal testers 'in addition to the requirements in paragraph 1', and 26(8) sends to Article 27: the in-house red team may test only if it meets them. Lead-in that turns points (a) to (e) into conditions; a specific provision the main rule refers to and the answer needs. Applies because the bank would use its staff as TLPT testers: 2.

'are of the highest suitability and reputability;' One of the requirements that 27(2) imposes on internal testers in addition to its own conditions; the in-house red team would be the testers, so if it fails this requirement it cannot be used. Condition that can change the answer: 2.

'possess technical and organisational capabilities and demonstrate specific expertise in threat intelligence, penetration testing and red team testing;' Requirement the in-house red team must meet as TLPT testers, applied to internal testers by 27(2) ('in addition to the requirements in paragraph 1'). Condition that can change the answer: 2.

'are certified by an accreditation body in a Member State or adhere to formal codes of conduct or ethical frameworks;' Requirement the in-house testers must meet under 27(2); an in-house team with neither certification nor a formal code fails it. Condition that can change the answer: 2.

'provide an independent assurance, or an audit report, in relation to the sound management of risks associated with the carrying out of TLPT, including the due protection of the financial entity's confidential information and redress for the business risks of the financial entity;' Requirement the in-house testers must also meet under 27(2). Condition that can change the answer: 2.

'are duly and fully covered by relevant professional indemnity insurances, including against risks of misconduct and negligence.' Requirement the in-house testers must also meet under 27(2). Condition that can change the answer: 2.

'When using internal testers, financial entities shall ensure that, in addition to the requirements in paragraph 1, the following conditions are met:' The rule that answers the question: a financial entity may use internal testers for TLPT if the listed conditions are met on top of 27(1). The need asks whether the bank may use its own staff, so the answer is this permission with conditions and it lives in the lead-in (as for the yes-or-no question in the 28(8) worked example); points (a) to (c) are the conditions (2). Applies on the stated facts: the bank, required to perform TLPT, wants its in-house red team as the testers. 3.

'such use has been approved by the relevant competent authority or by the single public authority designated in accordance with Article 26(9) and (10);' Without it the answer is wrong: the bank cannot simply decide to use its own staff, the use needs supervisory approval. Condition of the permission in 27(2), applying because the bank wants internal testers: 2.

'the relevant competent authority has verified that the financial entity has sufficient dedicated resources and ensured that conflicts of interest are avoided throughout the design and execution phases of the test;' Condition of the permission in 27(2): supervisory verification of resources and of the avoidance of conflicts of interest for the in-house team. Can change the answer: 2.

'the threat intelligence provider is external to the financial entity.' Condition of the permission in 27(2): even with an in-house red team as testers, the threat intelligence must come from an external provider, so the TLPT cannot be run wholly in-house. Can change the answer: 2.

'Financial entities shall ensure that contracts concluded with external testers require a sound management of the TLPT results ...' Governs contracts with external testers and does not decide whether in-house staff may test. Not a 0, because 26(8) obliges the bank to contract external testers every three tests (and always, if it is a significant credit institution), and those contracts fall under it: useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out: 1.

'ICT third-party service provider' means an undertaking providing ICT services. This is the term 31(8)(iv) uses for the company. A software company that provides an IT service to financial firms as its clients maps to it obviously, and the stated facts point to no other category (not a financial entity, no group). An answer cannot go wrong without it, so it is context.

'critical ICT third-party service provider' means an ICT third-party service provider designated as critical in accordance with Article 31. It maps the managers' 'critical IT provider' to the legal status and points to Article 31 as where to look. It says nothing on who can or cannot be designated, so a complete answer can leave it out.

31(1)(a), 'designate the ICT third-party service providers that are critical for financial entities, following an assessment that takes into account the criteria specified in paragraph 2', is the mechanism that 31(8) points to. Under the grade-3 test, the answering node 31(8)(iv) is read with the article heading 'Designation of critical ICT third-party service providers' and its lead-in 'The designation referred to in paragraph 1, point (a), shall not apply to the following', and that already says which designation the company falls outside of. So the answer is neither wrong nor incomplete without this node's content (who designates, and the paragraph 2 assessment), and since 'a cross-reference never adds qrels by itself' it is useful context a correct and complete answer can leave out (grade 1).

'the systemic impact ... taking into account the number of financial entities and the total value of assets of financial entities to which the relevant ICT third-party service provider provides services'. This is the criterion behind the managers' assumption that many financial firms use the service. It explains their premise, but the paragraph 2 criteria only matter for a provider that the designation can reach, and 31(8)(iv) takes this company out first. Useful context, not needed for the answer.

'shall not be used until the Commission has adopted a delegated act in accordance with paragraph 6' only fixes when the designation mechanism may start for any provider. On the stated facts (the service is provided only in one Member State, to clients active only there), 31(8) says 'The designation referred to in paragraph 1, point (a), shall not apply' to this company at all, so whatever the state of the delegated act this node can neither give nor change the answer under any reasonable reading of unstated facts. It is not an exception that the facts rule out but a timing bar on a designation that never reaches the company, and citing it would wrongly present a temporary bar as the reason: a hard negative that shares 31(8)'s opening words, graded 0 after the scope check.

'The designation referred to in paragraph 1, point (a), shall not apply to the following:'. This lead-in turns point (iv) into a rule: it carries the negation ('shall not apply') and ties the list to the designation as critical, which is what the need asks about. On its own it does not say which providers are excluded, so the answer for this company is in point (iv). It applies because the need asks whether the company can be designated under that designation. Grade 2 as the lead-in of a point that holds the answer (the 28(7) pattern).

'financial entities providing ICT services to other financial entities'. This is a sibling exclusion that the stated facts rule out: the company is a software company, not one of the entities of DORA 2(1)(a) to (t) that 2(2) calls financial entities. An exclusion ruled out by the facts is context. It would not change the answer in any case, since the answer rests on point (iv). It tempts lexically ('providing ICT services', 'financial entities').

'ICT third-party service providers that are subject to oversight frameworks established for the purposes of supporting the tasks referred to in Article 127(2) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union'. This is a sibling exclusion. The need does not say the company is under such a framework, and if it were, this would only add a second ground for the same 'no', so it cannot change the answer. It tempts lexically ('ICT third-party service providers', 'oversight'), but a complete answer can leave it out. Context.

'ICT intra-group service providers'. This is a sibling exclusion for undertakings that are part of a financial group and serve predominantly that group's financial entities (DORA 3(20)). The need describes a software company with many financial firms as clients and says nothing of a financial group. Even if that held, it would only add a second ground for the same answer. Context that a complete answer can leave out.

'ICT third-party service providers providing ICT services solely in one Member State to financial entities that are only active in that Member State.' Read with its lead-in ('The designation referred to in paragraph 1, point (a), shall not apply to the following') and the heading 'Designation of critical ICT third-party service providers', it answers directly: such a provider cannot be designated as critical. The stated facts establish both conditions. The company 'provides the service only there' (solely in one Member State), and 'all of its clients operate only in the EU country where the company is based' (financial entities only active in that Member State). So the answer is no, however many financial firms use the service.

'The ICT third-party service providers that are not included in the list referred to in paragraph 9 may request to be designated as critical in accordance with paragraph 1, point (a).' A provider not on the list could read this as a way in. But the request leads to designation 'in accordance with paragraph 1, point (a)', which is the very designation that 31(8) says 'shall not apply' to providers like the company, so the text closes this route and it cannot change the answer. Context that an answer may mention ('not even on request') but can leave out.

'A crypto-asset service provider shall be deemed significant if it has in the Union at least 15 million active users'. Hard negative from the parallel size-based regimes in MiCA. It tempts because it gives a service provider a special status for the number of its users, which is the managers' reasoning. It is wrong on the stated facts. It reaches only crypto-asset service providers (MiCA 3(1)(15): undertakings providing crypto-asset services to clients, allowed under Article 59), while the company is a software company providing an IT service to financial firms. The question is designation as critical ICT provider under DORA, which this node does not govern. It also brings no EU-level oversight: under 85(3), home competent authorities keep their responsibilities.

Under 'requirements applicable to financial entities in relation to:', point (v) names 'information and intelligence sharing in relation to cyber threats and vulnerabilities;'. It confirms that DORA regulates the subject of the need but states no condition for the sharing; a correct and complete answer can leave it out. Context.

'For the purposes of this Regulation, entities referred to in paragraph 1, points (a) to (t), shall collectively be referred to as 'financial entities'.' With 2(1)(a) 'credit institutions' it makes the bank a financial entity, the actor of 45(1), and it fixes the meaning of 'trusted communities of financial entities' in 45(1)(b). The mapping bank, credit institution, financial entity is obvious, the need states that the other members are financial firms, and it asks for the conditions, not whether a given member qualifies; condition (b) is stated correctly without the definition. Context, not necessary.

''cyber threat' means 'cyber threat' as defined in Article 2, point (8), of Regulation (EU) 2019/881' is a pointer to an act outside the corpus. The need's 'information about cyber threats, such as indicators of compromise and attackers' tactics' matches the wording of 45(1) itself ('cyber threat information and intelligence, including indicators of compromise, tactics, techniques, and procedures'), so the definition is not needed to decide whether the rule applies. Context.

''threat intelligence' means information that has been aggregated, transformed, analysed, interpreted or enriched ... including the technical details of a cyber-attack, those responsible for the attack and their modus operandi and motivations'. It covers the attackers' tactics of the need, but 45(1) already names 'indicators of compromise, tactics, techniques, and procedures' and does not use this defined term; no element of the answer depends on it. Context.

Art. 13(3) applies to the bank as a financial entity (2.2) and concerns the exchange the need describes ('relevant information exchanged with counterparts'). However, it only requires that this information 'shall be duly incorporated on a continuous basis into the ICT risk assessment process', which sets no condition on the sharing. A correct and complete answer can therefore leave it out, so it is useful context (grade 1). It is not a 0: 'neither answers nor changes the answer' is the test that rules out grade 2, while grade 0 needs 'definitely not relevant' and never 'probably not relevant', which a node about the same exchange does not meet.

'Financial entities may, on a voluntary basis, notify significant cyber threats to the relevant competent authority when they deem the threat to be of relevance to the financial system, service users or clients.' It tempts: the same permissive 'Financial entities may' for cyber threat information, with its own condition. It is wrong on the facts: the recipient is the relevant competent authority (sub_2: the national authority that forwards to the ECB; sub_3: CSIRTs where a Member State allows it), never the other firms of a group, and the need asks about sharing with the other members of a group of financial firms, which 45(1) governs. No reasonable unstated fact makes it govern that exchange. Parallel regime: the voluntary channel for cyber threat information to another recipient.

'Financial entities may exchange amongst themselves cyber threat information and intelligence, including indicators of compromise, tactics, techniques, and procedures, cyber security alerts and configuration tools, to the extent that such information and intelligence sharing:'. It grants the permission for exactly the information the need names and makes it conditional ('to the extent that'), but the conditions asked for are in points (a) to (c); as for the lead-in of 28(7) in the worked example, the lead-in that turns the points into conditions is a 2. Applies: the bank is a credit institution (2(1)(a)), hence a financial entity (2(2)), and wants to exchange indicators of compromise and attackers' tactics with other financial firms.

'aims to enhance the digital operational resilience of financial entities, in particular through raising awareness in relation to cyber threats, limiting or impeding the cyber threats' ability to spread, supporting defence capabilities, threat detection techniques, mitigation strategies or response and recovery stages;'. Read with the lead-in, it is one element of the list asked for: the purpose the sharing must pursue. Applies: the bank, a financial entity, wants to share the information the lead-in names (indicators of compromise, tactics) with a group of financial firms.

'takes places within trusted communities of financial entities;'. Read with the lead-in, it is one element of the list asked for: the circle within which the sharing may take place. Applies: the bank wants to share within a group of other financial firms.

'is implemented through information-sharing arrangements that protect the potentially sensitive nature of the information shared, and that are governed by rules of conduct in full respect of business confidentiality, protection of personal data in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and guidelines on competition policy.'. Read with the lead-in, it is one element of the list asked for: the arrangement and its rules of conduct. Applies: the bank's sharing would run through the group's arrangement. The content of Regulation 2016/679 and of the competition guidelines is outside the corpus, but the condition itself is stated here in full.

'For the purpose of paragraph 1, point (c), the information-sharing arrangements shall define the conditions for participation and, where appropriate, shall set out the details on the involvement of public authorities ..., on the involvement of ICT third-party service providers, and on operational elements, including the use of dedicated IT platforms.'. Not a separate condition but what an arrangement must contain to satisfy point (c): an answer that stated (c) without it would be incomplete, since the group's arrangement must define its conditions for participation. Applies: the bank would join and share through the group's arrangement; only the 'where appropriate' details depend on facts the need does not state (public authorities or ICT providers involved).

The stated facts trigger it: joining the group is participation in 'the information-sharing arrangements referred to in paragraph 1', and the bank 'shall notify competent authorities ... upon validation of their membership'. It is not one of the 45(1) 'to the extent that' conditions, so it is not a 3. It is, however, a mandatory duty in the same article and is tied to the participation through which the sharing takes place, so an answer that left it out 'would not be legally correct or complete' (section 2, grade 2). Calling it merely 'practical' treats a legal obligation as if it were advice.

'The ESAs, through the Joint Committee and in collaboration with competent authorities, ..., the ESRB and ENISA, as appropriate, may establish mechanisms to enable the sharing of effective practices across financial sectors to enhance situational awareness and identify common cyber vulnerabilities and risks across sectors.'. It tempts: mechanisms for sharing across financial sectors about cyber vulnerabilities. It is wrong on the facts: its actors are the ESAs and other authorities, it empowers them to set up mechanisms for sharing 'effective practices', and it sets no condition on a financial entity's exchange with its peers; 49.2 confirms the article deals with cooperation among authorities. The need's group is formed by financial firms, and even an authority-run mechanism would leave the bank's conditions to 45(1).

'Any confidential information received, exchanged or transmitted pursuant to this Regulation shall be subject to the conditions of professional secrecy laid down in paragraph 2.'. It tempts: read alone it seems to attach 'conditions' to any information exchanged under DORA, including exchanges under 45(1). It is wrong on the facts: paragraph 2 applies the obligation to 'all persons who work, or who have worked, for the competent authorities' and to those to whom the authorities have delegated their powers, and paragraphs 3 and 4 concern information held or exchanged by authorities; the bank and the other firms of the group are none of these, so it sets no condition on the bank's sharing. The confidentiality the sharing must respect comes from 45(1)(c).

'critical ICT third-party service provider' means an ICT third-party service provider designated as critical in accordance with Article 31. The need's 'designated under DORA as a critical IT provider' maps obviously onto this term and no other category is plausible; it confirms that Article 43 reaches the company, but an answer on the amount can leave the definition out. 1.

'Lead Overseer' means the European Supervisory Authority appointed in accordance with Article 31(1), point (b). It names who charges the fees under 43(1) ('The Lead Overseer shall ... charge'); useful context, but it says nothing on how much. 1.

'appoint as Lead Overseer for each critical ICT third-party service provider the ESA that is responsible ... for the financial entities having together the largest share of total assets'. It tells which ESA will charge the company's fees; context only, nothing on the amount. 1.

'The Oversight Forum may, where appropriate, seek the advice of independent experts appointed in accordance with paragraph 6.' 43(1) names 'the costs of advice provided by the independent experts as referred to in Article 32(4), second subparagraph' among the costs the fees cover; this node only says such advice may be sought. Context on one cost item; the cross-reference adds no relevance by itself. 1.

The node applies to the company but says nothing about fees. Still, the 'individual oversight plan describing the annual oversight objectives and the main oversight actions planned for each critical ICT third-party service provider', 'communicated yearly', is the yearly programme of oversight work whose cost the fees recover under 43.1 ('necessary expenditure in relation to the conduct of oversight tasks') and the second subparagraph of 43.1 ('all costs derived from the execution of the duties set out in this Section'), so it is not 'definitely not relevant' as grade 0 requires; it is useful context that an answer on the amount can leave out, which is grade 1.

'The amount of the periodic penalty payment ... shall be up to 1 % of the average daily worldwide turnover of the critical ICT third-party service provider in the preceding business year.' Tempts: it shares 'amount', 'turnover' and 'critical ICT third-party service provider' with Article 43 and gives the only figure tied to the provider, which an answer could wrongly present as the fee. Wrong on the facts: under 35(6) the penalty is imposed only 'in the event of whole or partial non-compliance' with measures under 35(1), points (a) to (c), 'to compel' compliance, daily for at most six months (35(7)), and its amounts go to 'the general budget of the European Union' (35(9)); it is a sanction, not the oversight fee that comes with the designation (43(1)). Non-compliance, if it happened, would not change the fee either. 0.

'the Lead Overseer shall be assisted by a joint examination team established for each critical ICT third-party service provider.' 43(1) includes 'the reimbursement of any costs which may be incurred as a result of work carried out by the joint examination team referred to in Article 40'; this node says such a team exists for each provider. Context on one cost item; an answer on the amount can leave it out. 1.

The stated designation makes the company a 'critical ICT third-party service provider' (3.23, 31.1.a), and the node imposes the fees and fixes their basis ('fees that fully cover the Lead Overseer's necessary expenditure in relation to the conduct of oversight tasks', joint examination team and expert costs included). But it states no amount or yearly figure and charges the fees 'in accordance with the delegated act referred to in paragraph 2', so it does not answer 'how much ... each year' directly and completely as grade 3 requires; without it the answer would be incomplete, and it says where the amount is fixed, which is grade 2.

'The amount of a fee charged to a critical ICT third-party service provider shall cover all costs derived from the execution of the duties set out in this Section and shall be proportionate to its turnover' applies to the designated company (3.23, 31.1.a) and is the corpus's core rule on the amount. But it gives no figure, rate or yearly amount, so it does not state the figure asked for directly and completely as grade 3 requires; a correct answer cannot leave out its cost-coverage and turnover-proportionality limits, which is grade 2.

'The Commission is empowered to adopt a delegated act in accordance with Article 57 to supplement this Regulation by determining the amount of the fees and the way in which they are to be paid by 17 July 2024.' It says where the element asked for is fixed: the amount, and how it is paid, live in a Commission delegated act outside the corpus (mandate rule: 2). Without it the answer would miss that DORA itself sets no figure. Applies to the fees charged to designated providers under 43(1), which the facts of the need establish. 2.

'The amount of the fee charged to an individual issuer of a significant e-money token shall be proportionate to the size of issuance of the e-money token in exchange for funds and shall cover all costs derived from the execution of EBA's supervisory tasks under this Regulation'. Tempts: almost the wording of DORA 43(1), second subparagraph ('The amount of a fee charged ... shall cover all costs derived from the execution of ... proportionate to'). Wrong: it is the parallel regime of another act and actor, the fees EBA charges to issuers of significant asset-referenced and e-money tokens (MiCA 137(1)); the need's company is a cloud provider designated under DORA and asks about the fees that come with that designation, which MiCA's fees are not on any reasonable reading of the facts. 0.

'The Commission shall adopt a delegated act in accordance with Article 139 by 30 June 2024 to supplement this Regulation by specifying further the type of fees, the matters for which fees are due, the amount of the fees and the manner in which they are to be paid and the methodology to calculate the maximum amount per entity ... that can be charged by EBA.' Tempts: twin of DORA 43(2), and its 'maximum amount per entity' looks like an answer to 'how much'. Wrong: it mandates MiCA's delegated act on the supervisory fees EBA charges to issuers of significant tokens (137(1)), not the DORA delegated act on oversight fees for designated ICT providers; citing it would send the finance director to the wrong Level 2 act and deadline. 0.

Lead-in 2(4) 'This Regulation does not apply to crypto-assets that qualify as one or more of the following:', point (a) 'financial instruments;'. The need states the token 'is not a financial instrument', so the exclusion is ruled out by the stated facts and cannot change the answer (exceptions rule): context confirming that MiCA applies. 1.

The need's own fact 'The token is not a stablecoin' maps directly onto the definition's words 'purports to maintain a stable value', so the facts already rule out the exclusion in MiCA:11.1 ('other than asset-referenced tokens or e-money tokens'), and the answer rests on MiCA:8.3 ('shall not require prior approval of crypto-asset white papers') whether or not this definition is read. Section 2 applies: an obvious mapping from everyday words to the legal term is not a 2 by default, and a condition that the need's facts rule out is a 1, so this is useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out.

'purports to maintain a stable value by referencing the value of one official currency' is the plainest sense of 'stablecoin', so the need's 'not a stablecoin' already excludes it by an obvious mapping. Because the e-money-token twin (51(11)) also bars prior approval, the classification would change the cited article but not the answer, so a correct and complete answer can leave it out (section 2, Definitions: an obvious mapping is not a 2 by default): 1.

'A person shall not make an offer to the public ... unless that person:' sets necessary conditions for the offer, none of them an approval, so it supports the answer only by omission and does not state the rule, which 8(3) does. The point it would turn into a rule here, notification under (c), does not change the answer, so the lead-in case of section 2 does not raise it: useful context, 1.

Read with 4(1), the offer requires that the person 'has notified the crypto-asset white paper in accordance with Article 8'.
