'Paragraph 1, points (b), (c), (d) and (f), shall not apply to any of the following offers to the public of crypto-assets other than asset-referenced tokens or e-money tokens:' (fewer than 150 persons per Member State, EUR 1 000 000 over 12 months, qualified investors only). The need does not give the size or audience of the offer, so it could apply, but it only lifts the duties to draw up, notify and publish; it creates no approval, and a white paper drawn up anyway stays under the Title (4(8)). It cannot change the answer: 1.

'This Title shall not apply to offers to the public of crypto-assets other than asset-referenced tokens or e-money tokens where any of the following apply:' (offered for free, validation reward, utility token for an existing good or service, limited network). Unstated facts could bring the offer here, but then Title II would simply not apply and no approval would arise either; a voluntary white paper falls back under the Title (4(8)). Does not change the answer: 1.

Under the lead-in of 6(3) the white paper must carry 'This crypto-asset white paper has not been approved by any competent authority in any Member State of the European Union', which presupposes and corroborates the answer but is a content requirement, not the rule on approval. The answer resting on 8(3) is correct and complete without it (section 2, grade 1): 1.

'shall notify their crypto-asset white paper to the competent authority of their home Member State' is the duty owed instead of an approval request, but it neither answers whether approval is required nor changes that answer. Its scope words ('crypto-assets other than asset-referenced tokens or e-money tokens') repeat the Title II scope that 4(1) already gives, and the need asks only about approval, so this is useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out (section 2, grade 1): 1.

'Competent authorities shall not require prior approval of crypto-asset white papers, nor of any marketing communications relating thereto, before their respective publication.' Read with its heading 'Notification of the crypto-asset white paper and of the marketing communications', it answers the primary question directly: no, the regulator does not approve the white paper. The stated facts establish that it applies: an offer to the public in the EU of a crypto-asset that is not a financial instrument (MiCA applies, 2(4)(a)) and not a stablecoin (neither ART nor EMT, 3(1)(6), 3(1)(7)), so a Title II white paper, the one Article 8 governs (8(1)). The negation carries the answer: 3.

'at least 20 working days before the date of publication of the crypto-asset white paper' is a lead time for the notification, not a review or approval period. It times a separate duty and does not change the answer to the approval question (section 2, grade 1): 1.

8(3) bars approval 'before their respective publication', while the need asks about approval before the offer goes ahead. 'After publication of the crypto-asset white paper in accordance with Article 9 ... offerors may offer crypto-assets other than asset-referenced tokens or e-money tokens throughout the Union' makes publication, not any approval, what opens the offer, and the founders are offerors (3(1)(13)) of such a crypto-asset, so without it the answer covers publication but not the launch (section 2, grade 2): 2.

Under 17(1) 'An asset-referenced token issued by a credit institution may be offered to the public or admitted to trading if the credit institution:': 'draws up a crypto-asset white paper ... submits that crypto-asset white paper for approval by the competent authority of its home Member State ... and has the crypto-asset white paper approved by the competent authority'. It tempts because it is exactly the approval before the offer that the founders assume. It is the parallel regime for asset-referenced tokens issued by credit institutions; the founders' token is not a stablecoin, hence not an asset-referenced token (3(1)(6)). Definitely not relevant on the stated facts: 0.

'Competent authorities shall, within 25 working days ... take a fully reasoned decision granting or refusing authorisation to the applicant issuer ... Where an applicant issuer is authorised, its crypto-asset white paper shall be deemed to be approved.' It tempts with a white paper approved by the authority. An 'applicant issuer' is an issuer of asset-referenced tokens or e-money tokens applying for authorisation (3(1)(11)), the authorisation 16(1) requires for asset-referenced tokens; the founders' token is not a stablecoin, so not an ART (3(1)(6)). Definitely not relevant on the stated facts: 0.

'Competent authorities shall not require prior approval of crypto-asset white papers before their publication.' Near-identical to 8(3) and with the same verdict, but it sits in Article 51 'Content and form of the crypto-asset white paper for e-money tokens', after 51(11) 'Issuers of e-money tokens shall notify their crypto-asset white paper ...', a regime open only to issuers authorised as credit or electronic money institutions (48(1)(a)). The founders' token is not a stablecoin, hence not an e-money token (3(1)(7)); the rule for their white paper is 8(3). Lexical twin, the wrong article on the stated facts: 0.

Under 140(2) 'The reports referred to in paragraph 1 shall contain the following:' (the Commission's reports, 140(1)): 'an assessment of the necessity of the introduction of an approval mechanism for crypto-asset white papers for crypto-assets other than asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens;'. A reporting duty of the Commission, not a rule for offerors; it presupposes that no approval mechanism exists for the founders' kind of white paper. Context a correct and complete answer can leave out: 1.

Defines "'asset-referenced token'" as a crypto-asset "that is not an electronic money token and that purports to maintain a stable value by referencing another value or right or a combination thereof, including one or more official currencies". A token tied to a basket of several currencies and gold is such a combination, so this definition is what puts the need under Art 39 instead of the e-money regime of Art 49, whose answer differs (par value, always cash). A definition needed to decide which rule applies: 2. It applies because the need states the basket of currencies and gold.

"'electronic money token' ... means a type of crypto-asset that purports to maintain a stable value by referencing the value of one official currency". 'Stablecoin' covers both categories and 3.1.6 excludes e-money tokens, so this is the line that rules out the e-money regime (49.4, 'at any time and at par value') for a token tied to several currencies and gold. It separates two plausible legal categories with different answers; without it the need can reasonably be answered under the wrong regime: 2.

"'retail holder' means any natural person who is acting for purposes which are outside that person's trade, business, craft or profession". Names the investor's legal category, but 39.1 gives the right to "Holders of asset-referenced tokens" with no retail distinction, and the term is used only for the right of withdrawal (Art 13) and supervisory powers. Context; a complete answer can leave it out.

"Retail holders who purchase crypto-assets other than asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens ... shall have a right of withdrawal." Tempts because it is a retail holder's right to give crypto-assets back and be reimbursed (13.2). Wrong on the stated facts: it excludes asset-referenced tokens, and a token tied to several currencies and gold is one (3.1.6); it is also a 14-day withdrawal from the purchase (13.1.sub_2), not a standing right of redemption.

Read under its lead-in (Art 19(6), the summary of the crypto-asset white paper for asset-referenced tokens), the node only sets what the summary 'shall state': 'that the holders of asset-referenced tokens have a right of redemption at any time, and the conditions for such redemption'. It repeats the right without granting or qualifying it, and it states no condition of its own, so under 'Twins and repeated wording' (only the right article, Art 39, is relevant) it is graded 0. Scope check passed: the rule binds whoever drafts the white paper, and no unstated fact would make a rule on the summary's content answer or change whether she may redeem at any time.

Under its scope provision 29(1) the article governs 'marketing communications relating to an offer to the public of an asset-referenced token', and 29(2) only requires them to 'contain a clear and unambiguous statement that the holders of the asset-referenced token have a right of redemption against the issuer at any time'. It repeats the wording of the right without creating or qualifying it, so under 'Twins and repeated wording' it is graded 0. Scope check passed: no unstated fact would make a content requirement for marketing communications answer or change her entitlement.

"describe the procedure to purchase asset-referenced tokens and to redeem such tokens against the reserve of assets, and list the persons or categories of persons who are entitled to do so". Tempts with 'redeem' and 'entitled', but it is content of the stabilisation-mechanism policy (36.8) on redeeming against the reserve of assets; it does not narrow the right of every holder "at all times against the issuers" (39.1), which reaches the reserve assets only when issuers cannot meet their obligations. Context.

"Holders of asset-referenced tokens shall have a right of redemption at all times against the issuers of the asset-referenced tokens, and in respect of the reserve assets when issuers are not able to meet their obligations". Answers the primary question directly: yes, a right of redemption against the issuer at all times. It applies because she holds a token whose value is tied to several currencies and gold, an asset-referenced token under 3.1.6 and not an e-money token under 3.1.7.

"Upon request by a holder of an asset-referenced token, an issuer of such token shall redeem either by paying an amount in funds, other than electronic money, equivalent to the market value of the assets referenced by the asset-referenced token held or by delivering the assets referenced by the token." Answers the 'take back her tokens and pay her out' part directly: on her request the issuer must redeem, paying the market value of the basket (not a fixed par) or handing over the referenced assets. Same applicability as 39.1. Its second sentence is the lead-in of policy points (a) to (e).

Under the lead-in "Issuers shall establish a policy on such permanent right of redemption setting out:", point (a): "the conditions, including thresholds, periods and timeframes, for holders of asset-referenced tokens to exercise such right of redemption". The exercise of the right is subject to thresholds, periods and timeframes set by the issuer: a condition that qualifies 'at any time she chooses'. Applies to every ART issuer; the content of the policy is not stated: 2.

"the mechanisms and procedures to ensure the redemption of the asset-referenced tokens, including in stressed market circumstances, as well as in the context of the implementation of the recovery plan set out in Article 46 or, in the case of an orderly redemption of asset-referenced tokens, under Article 47". Policy content that marks where to look (Arts 46 and 47); it neither grants nor limits the right. Context.

The node only says that an issuer which accepts 'a payment in funds other than electronic money, denominated in an official currency' must 'always provide an option to redeem the token in funds other than electronic money, denominated in the same official currency'; it fixes the currency of the pay-out for buyers who paid in fiat, not whether or when she can redeem, which is what the need asks and what 39.1 ('at all times'), 39.2.a and Article 46 settle. Under section 2 it does not answer a primary question and does not change the yes or no answer (the condition-or-exception test of grade 2 is not met), so a correct and complete answer can leave it out: grade 1.

"Without prejudice to Article 46, the redemption of asset-referenced tokens shall not be subject to a fee." The need asks whether and when she can redeem, not what it costs: context. Its reference to Article 46 marks where to look; the Art 46 nodes are graded on their own.

"An issuer of an asset-referenced token shall draw up and maintain a recovery plan providing for measures to be taken by the issuer to restore compliance with the requirements applicable to the reserve of assets in cases where the issuer fails to comply with those requirements." The duty to have the plan; the circumstances in which the recovery measures and the authority's suspension apply are stated in full in 46.3, so the answer can leave this node out. Context.

"The recovery plan shall include appropriate conditions and procedures to ensure the timely implementation of recovery actions as well as a wide range of recovery options, including:". The lead-in that makes points (b) daily limits and (c) suspension of redemptions required recovery options; without it they are bare nouns. Applies if the issuer fails or is likely to fail its reserve requirements (46.1, 46.3), a fact the need does not state that could reasonably hold: 2.

"liquidity fees on redemptions". A recovery option that affects what redemption costs (the counterpart of 39.3's 'Without prejudice to Article 46'), not whether or when she can redeem, which is what the need asks. Context.

"limits on the amount of the asset-referenced token that can be redeemed on any working day". Under the recovery plan she may not be able to redeem all her tokens on the day she chooses: an exception to 'at all times'. Applies only if the issuer fails or is likely to fail its reserve requirements and the plan is implemented (46.1, 46.3), a fact not stated that could reasonably hold: 2.

"suspension of redemptions." A recovery option that stops redemption altogether, the direct exception to 'at any time she chooses'. Same unstated fact that could reasonably hold (issuer in or near breach of its reserve requirements): 2.

"Where the issuer fails to comply with the requirements applicable to the reserve of assets ... or, due to a rapidly deteriorating financial condition, is likely in the near future to not comply with those requirements, the competent authority ... shall have the power to require the issuer to implement one or more of the arrangements or measures set out in the recovery plan". The condition of the exceptions: it fixes when the recovery measures (including limits and suspension of redemptions) can be imposed, and it is 'the circumstances referred to in paragraph 3' on which 46.4 depends. Without it the exception cannot be stated correctly: 2.

"In the circumstances referred to in paragraph 3, the competent authority shall have the power to temporarily suspend the redemption of asset-referenced tokens, provided that the suspension is justified having regard to the interests of the holders of asset-referenced tokens and financial stability." An exception to the right 'at all times': while a suspension lasts she cannot redeem when she chooses. Applies only if the issuer fails or is likely to fail its reserve requirements, a fact the need does not state that could reasonably hold: 2.

"an operational plan to support the orderly redemption of each asset-referenced token, which is to be implemented upon a decision by the competent authority that the issuer is unable or likely to be unable to fulfil its obligations, including in the case of insolvency". The mechanism behind 39.1's right 'in respect of the reserve assets when issuers are not able to meet their obligations as referred to in Chapter 6'; 39.1 already states that fallback, so this is context.

"Upon request by a holder of an e-money token, the issuer of that e-money token shall redeem it, at any time and at par value, by paying in funds, other than electronic money, the monetary value of the e-money token held". The parallel regime of 39.2 for e-money tokens, and close to the need's words ('at any time', 'paying'). Wrong on the stated facts: it reaches only e-money tokens, which reference 'the value of one official currency' (3.1.7); a token tied to several currencies and gold is an asset-referenced token (3.1.6). Applied, it would give a wrong answer (par value, always cash).

"Marketing communications shall contain a clear and unambiguous statement that the holders of the e-money token have a right of redemption against the issuer at any time and at par value." Tempts with 'right of redemption against the issuer at any time'. Wrong on the stated facts: it is a content rule for marketing communications on 'an offer to the public of an e-money token' (53.1), and her token is an asset-referenced token (3.1.6, 3.1.7); it also creates no right.

''asset-referenced token' means a type of crypto-asset that is not an electronic money token and that purports to maintain a stable value by referencing another value or right or a combination thereof, including one or more official currencies'. Its words 'one or more official currencies' can tempt a reader to file a euro stablecoin here, and its exclusion 'is not an electronic money token' is what keeps the token out of Title III (Article 16). Useful context for the classification, but 3(1)(7) alone places a token referencing the euro in the e-money token category, so a correct answer can leave this definition out: 1.

''electronic money token' or 'e-money token' means a type of crypto-asset that purports to maintain a stable value by referencing the value of one official currency'. The need says 'stablecoin, pegged one-to-one to the euro', which is not a legal term and could be taken for an asset-referenced token (Article 16, open to an authorised non-bank legal person under Article 21) or for another crypto-asset (Article 4, white paper only). This definition decides that the token is an e-money token and therefore that Article 48 governs; without it the need can be answered wrongly. What makes it apply: the token references the value of one official currency, the euro. Grade 2.

'A person shall not make an offer to the public of a crypto-asset other than an asset-referenced token or e-money token in the Union unless that person: (a) is a legal person; ...'. Tempting: the same 'shall not make an offer to the public ... unless' wording, with conditions (legal person, white paper) that an unlicensed start-up could meet, so a retriever can take it for the answer. Its own text reaches only crypto-assets 'other than an asset-referenced token or e-money token', and a token referencing the value of the euro alone is an e-money token (3(1)(7)). Parallel regime for another instrument, ruled out by the stated facts: 0.

'A person shall not make an offer to the public, or seek the admission to trading, of an asset-referenced token, within the Union, unless that person is the issuer of that asset-referenced token and is:'. Twin of 48(1) in near-identical words for asset-referenced tokens; under it a legal person established in the Union could be authorised under Article 21 (point (a)), which would give a different answer. An asset-referenced token is 'a type of crypto-asset that is not an electronic money token' (3(1)(6)), and the euro-pegged token is an e-money token (3(1)(7)), so the node does not reach it: 0.

Under the lead-in 'Paragraph 1 shall not apply where:', 'over a period of 12 months, calculated at the end of each calendar day, the average outstanding value of the asset-referenced token issued by an issuer never exceeds EUR 5 000 000 ... and the issuer is not linked to a network of other exempt issuers'. Tempting for a start-up as a small-issuer escape from the authorisation duty, with 'EUR' echoing the euro peg. It lifts only Article 16(1), which reaches asset-referenced tokens; the token is an e-money token (3(1)(7)), excluded from that category by 3(1)(6), and the exemptions of the e-money token regime are those of 48(4) and 48(5): 0.

The lead-in 'A person shall not make an offer to the public ... of an e-money token, within the Union, unless that person is the issuer of such e-money token and:' ends in 'and:'. It does not state the licence condition the start-up fails, because that condition sits in the point the lead-in governs, so the lead-in does not answer the need directly and completely. Section 2 lists 'the lead-in that turns a point into a rule' as grade 2, and being indispensable to the negative answer is the grade-2 test ('without it the answer would not be legally correct'), not the grade-3 one.

Read with the lead-in of 48(1): 'is authorised as a credit institution or as an electronic money institution; and'. This is the condition the stated facts decide: a start-up that 'holds no financial licence of any kind' is neither, so as it stands it may not offer its token, and the point also says what it would need. The lead-in alone ('unless ... and:') cannot tell whether the start-up is barred, so this point holds part of the answer directly. What makes it apply: no licence of any kind, an e-money token offered to the public in the EU. Grade 3.

'has notified a crypto-asset white paper to the competent authority and has published that crypto-asset white paper' is joined by 'and' to point (a), which the stated fact 'holds no financial licence of any kind' already fails, so the answer to whether the start-up is allowed 'as it stands today' stays no whatever its white paper status. Under section 2 a condition is 2 only when it 'would change the answer', and the need asks for no list of requirements, so this is useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out: 1.

'Notwithstanding the first subparagraph, upon the written consent of the issuer, other persons may offer to the public or seek the admission to trading of the e-money token.' A derogation for persons other than the issuer, who offer the token of an issuer with its consent. The need states that the start-up will issue and offer its own token, so the facts rule the derogation out; by the rule for exceptions ruled out by the facts: 1.
'E-money tokens shall be deemed to be electronic money.' Explains why the licences named in 48(1)(a) are the electronic money ones, but the answer stands on 48(1) without it: 1.

'An e-money token that references an official currency of a Member State shall be deemed to be offered to the public in the Union.' A euro token is deemed offered in the Union, which settles the territorial element of 48(1); the need already states an offer to the public in the EU, so the deeming adds nothing the answer needs: 1.

'Titles II and III of Directive 2009/110/EC shall apply with respect to e-money tokens unless otherwise stated in this Title.' Points to the e-money directive, outside the corpus, where the authorisation regime of electronic money institutions lies; it marks where to look for how to obtain the licence, not whether the start-up may issue today: 1.

'Paragraph 1 of this Article shall not apply to issuers of e-money tokens exempted in accordance with Article 9(1) of Directive 2009/110/EC' lifts the prohibition only for issuers that hold the e-money waiver status. The corpus text quoted in the record describes that status as 'an electronic money institution benefitting from a waiver', which is a regulated e-money status that a start-up which 'holds no financial licence of any kind' as it stands today does not have. The need states the licence position, so this is not a missing fact: the stated facts rule the exception out, and section 2 grades it 1 ('1 when the facts of the need rule them out').

'This Title, with the exception of paragraph 7 of this Article and Article 51, shall not apply in respect of e-money tokens exempt pursuant to Article 1(4) and (5) of Directive 2009/110/EC.' If the start-up's token fell within those exclusions of the e-money directive (for instance a token usable only within a limited network), the whole Title, the prohibition of 48(1) included, would not apply and the answer would change to: allowed without a licence, subject to the white paper of 48(7) and Article 51. The need does not say how the token can be used, and a tech start-up's own token could reasonably be built that way; the licence fact does not rule it out, because the exemption attaches to the token, not to the issuer's status. Grade 2. The conditions of the exclusions lie outside the corpus (Directive 2009/110/EC; the PSD2 Article 3 exclusions behind them are EXCLUDED).

'Issuers of e-money tokens shall, at least 40 working days before the date on which they intend to offer to the public those e-money tokens or seek their admission to trading, notify their competent authority of that intention.' A procedural notice for issuers that may offer; it does not decide whether an unlicensed start-up may issue: 1.

'Where paragraph 4 or 5 applies, the issuers of e-money tokens shall draw up a crypto-asset white paper and notify' it. Paragraph 4 is ruled out by 'no financial licence of any kind', but paragraph 5 turns on whether the token is one of the 'e-money tokens exempt pursuant to Article 1(4) and (5) of Directive 2009/110/EC', a fact about the kind of instrument that the need does not state and that could reasonably hold. On that route, paragraph 7 turns 'no authorisation needed' into 'no authorisation needed, but a white paper must be drawn up and notified'. Because 48(5) only names paragraph 7 without stating what it requires, paragraph 7 is 'a specific provision that the main rule refers to and that the answer needs', and under the applicability rule it is graded 2.

'Issuers of e-money tokens shall issue e-money tokens at par value and on the receipt of funds.' It matches 'issue' and the one-to-one peg, but it says how an e-money token must be issued, not who may issue it: 1.

'Crypto-asset service providers operating a trading platform for crypto-assets shall not deal on own account on the trading platform for crypto-assets they operate'. Tempts: a ban on own-account dealing tied to a crypto exchange, and the need is about exchange staff buying 'for herself'. Wrong on the stated facts: the duty binds the service provider itself (3(1)(15): a legal person or other undertaking) and only for dealing on the platform it operates; the buyer is an employee, a natural person, who bought on another platform. Whether her purchase is market abuse is decided by Title VI, not by this organisational rule.

'This Title shall apply to acts carried out by any person concerning crypto-assets that are admitted to trading or in respect of which a request for admission to trading has been made.' The scope condition of the market abuse rules: without it the answer cannot say that they reach her purchase, since the general scope of 2(1) speaks of issuers, offerors and service providers, not of a private buyer. The need establishes it: the token is 'already traded on other crypto platforms' and her employer is about to list it, and 'any person' covers an employee acting for herself. A condition, not the answer: 2.

'This Title shall also apply to any transaction, order or behaviour concerning crypto-assets as referred to in paragraph 1, irrespective of whether such transaction, order or behaviour takes place on a trading platform.' The need stresses that she bought 'on another platform' and does not say what kind of platform it is; if it is not a trading platform for crypto-assets (for example a broker selling from its own inventory), which could reasonably hold, this paragraph is what keeps the purchase inside the Title. It is also the provision that settles that the place of the purchase does not matter. Applies under an unstated fact that could reasonably hold: 2.

'This Title shall apply to actions and omissions, in the Union and in third countries, concerning crypto-assets as referred to in paragraph 1.' The need does not say where the other platform is; if it is outside the Union, which could reasonably hold for a crypto platform, this paragraph is what subjects her purchase to the prohibition, and without it the answer could wrongly be 'no'. Applies under an unstated fact that could reasonably hold: 2.

'For the purposes of this Regulation, inside information shall comprise the following types of information:' The lead-in that turns point (a) into the definition of inside information, the term on which the prohibition turns. Not the answer, but needed with point (a): 2.

'information of a precise nature, which has not been made public, relating, directly or indirectly, ... to one or more crypto-assets, and which, if it were made public, would likely have a significant effect on the prices of those crypto-assets'. The definition needed to decide whether the coming listing is inside information, and the need gives every element: she learned it 'before any public announcement' (not public), it concerns the token (relates to a crypto-asset), and 'Listings on her employer's platform usually make a token's price jump' (likely significant price effect). Without it the prohibition cannot be applied: 2.

'for persons charged with the execution of orders for crypto-assets on behalf of clients, it also means information of a precise nature conveyed by a client and relating to the client's pending orders in crypto-assets'. Tempts: same paragraph and almost the same wording as point (a), and it targets staff of crypto-asset service providers. Wrong on the stated facts: what she knew was her employer's coming listing, not information conveyed by a client about pending orders, so this type of inside information is not the one at stake whatever her job is.

'information shall be deemed to be of a precise nature if it indicates ... an event which has occurred or which may reasonably be expected to occur, where it is specific enough to enable a conclusion to be drawn as to the possible effect of that set of circumstances or event on the prices of crypto-assets.' The listing had not happened yet: her employer 'would soon list' the token. This paragraph is what makes a future event precise information; without it an answer could wrongly hold that a listing not yet carried out is not precise. The need also makes the price effect inferable ('usually make a token's price jump'). 2.

'An intermediate step in a protracted process shall be deemed to be inside information if, in and of itself, it satisfies the criteria of inside information referred to in paragraph 2.' Useful context: the need states the listing itself as the information ('would soon list'), not an intermediate step of a listing process, so a correct and complete answer can leave this paragraph out: 1.

'information which, if it were made public, would likely have a significant effect on the prices of crypto-assets shall mean information that a reasonable holder of crypto-assets would likely use as part of the basis of the holder's investment decisions.' The legal test of the price-effect element of point (a); the need supplies the fact for it ('Listings on her employer's platform usually make a token's price jump'), and a complete answer applies this test to it rather than the plain words alone. 2.

'insider dealing shall be deemed to arise where a person possesses inside information and uses that information by acquiring or disposing of, for its own account or for the account of a third party, directly or indirectly, crypto-assets to which that information relates.' Read with the heading 'Prohibition of insider dealing', it classifies exactly the conduct of the need: she held the non-public listing information and, before the announcement, acquired 'for herself' (own account) the token it relates to. 'directly or indirectly' and 'crypto-assets to which that information relates' also answer that buying on a platform other than her employer's changes nothing. Answers the primary question: 3.

'No person shall engage or attempt to engage in insider dealing or use inside information about crypto-assets to acquire, or dispose of, those crypto-assets, directly or indirectly, whether for that person's own account or for the account of a third party.' The prohibition itself: buying the token for herself while holding the non-public listing information is using inside information to acquire those crypto-assets for her own account. The stated facts establish that it applies (token traded on crypto platforms, 86.1; information obtained at work, 89.5.c). The answer, stated as a prohibition: 3.

'This Article applies to any person who possesses inside information as a result of:' The lead-in that, with point (c), fixes that the prohibition reaches her; without it point (c) is a loose phrase. Lead-in of the applicable condition: 2.

'having access to the information through the exercise of an employment, profession or duties'. The need says she 'learned at work' as an employee of the exchange: this point establishes that Article 89 applies to her as such, with no need to show that she knew or ought to have known it was inside information (the test of the second subparagraph). A condition of application the answer needs: 2.

'This Article also applies to any person who possesses inside information under circumstances other than those referred to in the first subparagraph where that person knows or ought to know that it is inside information.' The catch-all for persons outside points (a) to (d); the stated facts place her under point (c), so a correct and complete answer can leave it out: 1.

'No person in possession of inside information shall unlawfully disclose inside information to any other person, except where such disclosure is made in the normal exercise of an employment, a profession or duties.' Tempts: the sibling prohibition of the same Title, on inside information, and its employment exception echoes how she learned the information. Wrong on the stated facts: it forbids passing inside information to another person; the need asks about her own purchase and states no disclosure, and the employment exception cannot cover a purchase.

Point (a) 'financial instruments;' under the lead-in 'This Regulation does not apply to crypto-assets that qualify as one or more of the following:'. If the coin were a financial instrument, MiCA, and with it Article 103, would not apply. 'Where the entities referred to in paragraphs 1 to 6 of this Article provide crypto-asset services, they shall not be subject to Articles 62, 63, 64, 67, 83 and 84.' The stated facts rule the exclusion out, so under section 2 (exceptions) it is a 1, not a 2.

'Any natural or legal person or such persons acting in concert who have taken a decision either to acquire, directly or indirectly, ... a qualifying holding in a crypto-asset service provider ... shall notify the competent authority of that crypto-asset service provider thereof in writing indicating the size of the intended holding and the information required pursuant to the regulatory technical standards ...'. The stated facts establish that it applies: the fund plans to buy 25 % of the shares (a qualifying holding under 3(1)(36)) of a crypto exchange authorised under MiCA (a crypto-asset service provider), and that authorisation rules out the Article 60(10) exclusion: 3.

'Where the competent authority does not oppose the proposed acquisition referred to in paragraph 1 before the date referred to in paragraph 4 ... the proposed acquisition shall be deemed to be approved.' The need states that she did nothing dishonest, so it does not change the answer; useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out: 1.

The need does not state this and it could reasonably hold, so 2.

'Credit institutions classified as significant ... shall report major ICT-related incidents to the relevant national competent authority designated in accordance with Article 4 of Directive 2013/36/EU, which shall immediately transmit that report to the ECB.' Hard negative: same paragraph and same duty with a different recipient route, i.e. the parallel regime for significant credit institutions, and it tempts a 'different authority (ECB)' answer. The node names its own actor, and the need's firm is a payment institution (DORA 3(35), PSD2 4(4)), not a credit institution (DORA 3(31)): 0.

'... produce ... the initial notification and reports referred to in paragraph 4 of this Article using the templates referred to in Article 20 and submit them to the competent authority. In the event that a technical impossibility prevents the submission ... notify the competent authority about it via alternative means.' It repeats the addressee fixed by the first subparagraph and adds the form (templates) and a fallback channel; the answer on which authority does not need it: context, 1.

'Without prejudice to the reporting pursuant to the first subparagraph by the financial entity to the relevant competent authority, Member States may additionally determine that some or all financial entities shall also provide the initial notification and each report ... to the competent authorities or the computer security incident response teams (CSIRTs) designated or established in accordance with Directive (EU) 2022/2555.' If the firm's Member State has used this option, a different authority (NIS2 authority or CSIRT) must also receive the report, on top of the competent authority. The need does not state the Member State or its choice, and it could reasonably hold: a condition that would change the answer, so 2.

'Financial entities shall, within the time limits to be laid down in accordance with Article 20, first paragraph, point (a), point (ii), submit the following to the relevant competent authority:' It lists which reports go (initial notification, intermediate, final) and repeats 'the relevant competent authority', which only 19(1) ties to Article 46. It adds nothing to the identity of the recipient; the answer can leave it out: 1.

'the ECB, in the case of financial entities referred to in Article 2(1), points (a), (b) and (d);' read with its lead-in 'Upon receipt of the initial notification and of each report referred to in paragraph 4, the competent authority shall, in a timely manner, provide details of the major ICT-related incident to the following recipients'. Point (b) of Article 2(1) is payment institutions, so the ECB gets details of this incident, but from the competent authority, not as the firm's report. It tempts a 'different authority' answer; it is useful context (the firm does not report to the ECB itself) that a complete answer can leave out: 1.

'The requirements laid down in this Chapter shall also apply to operational or security payment-related incidents and to major operational or security payment-related incidents, where they concern credit institutions, payment institutions, ...' The PI-specific article of the incident chapter: it extends the same reporting route to payment-related incidents. The need's incident is ICT-related, so Article 19 already applies and the recipient is the same either way: context, 1.

Lead-in: 'compliance with this Regulation shall be ensured by the following competent authorities in accordance with the powers granted by the respective legal acts:' It turns point (b) into the rule that the PSD2 Article 22 authority is the DORA competent authority for payment institutions; without it (b) is a bare list item (worked example of section 2). Applies because 19(1) refers to Article 46 and the firm is a payment institution: 2.

'for credit institutions and for institutions exempted pursuant to Directive 2013/36/EU, the competent authority designated in accordance with Article 4 of that Directive, and for credit institutions classified as significant ..., the ECB ...' Hard negative and parallel regime: the same allocation of the competent authority, for credit institutions; it would answer if the firm were a bank. The node names its actors, and the need's firm is a licensed payment institution (DORA 3(35), PSD2 4(4)), not a credit institution (DORA 3(31)) or a CRD-exempted institution (DORA 3(32)): 0.

Under the heading 'Competent authorities', point (b) names, for 'payment institutions' (the need's actor via DORA:3.35 and PSD2:4.4), 'the competent authority designated in accordance with Article 22 of Directive (EU) 2015/2366', but it states no reporting rule and does not by itself say whether that authority is the one that licensed the firm; it becomes the report's recipient only through Art. 19(1)'s 'relevant competent authority as referred to in Article 46', a cross-reference and not the lead-in that governs point (b). It is therefore 'a specific provision that the main rule refers to and that the answer needs' (section 2, grade 2; references to whole articles: 2 for the specific node without which the answer would be wrong or incomplete), not the grade-3 statement of the rule asked for.

'Competent authorities shall grant an authorisation if the information and evidence accompanying the application complies with all of the requirements laid down in Article 5 and if the competent authorities' overall assessment ... is favourable.' It shows that the licence is granted by the PSD2 competent authorities, but 22(1) already ties the Article 22 authorities to authorisation, so the answer can leave it out: context, 1. (Its reference to the EXCLUDED Article 5 plays no part in the grade.)

'Member States shall designate as the competent authorities responsible for the authorisation and prudential supervision of payment institutions which are to carry out the duties provided for under this Title ...' The specific provision DORA 46(b) refers to: it says the Article 22 authority is the one responsible for the authorisation (the licence) and prudential supervision of payment institutions, which is what lets the answer say 'the same authority that granted the licence'. Without it the answer could not settle same-or-different. It says nothing about incident reports, so it is not the answer by itself: 2 as the referred provision the answer needs. Applies because the firm is a licensed payment institution.

'Member States on whose territories there is more than one competent authority for matters covered by this Title shall ensure that those authorities cooperate closely ...' It shows that a Member State may have more than one PSD2 authority, i.e. that the condition of DORA 19(1) second subparagraph can hold; the operative rule is that DORA subparagraph, so this is context: 1.

'The tasks of the competent authorities designated under paragraph 1 shall be the responsibility of the competent authorities of the home Member State.' It confirms that the Article 22 authority is the home Member State's, consistent with the authority that authorised the firm; 22(1) already identifies the authorisation authority, so a correct and complete answer can leave it out: 1.

'Member States shall designate competent authorities to ensure and monitor effective compliance with this Directive.' Hard negative: same article title as DORA 46 ('Competent authorities') and a PSD2 designation of competent authorities, so it tempts as 'the PSD2 authority'. But DORA 46(b) names the authority designated under Article 22, not Article 100, and 100(4) ties these authorities to infringements of Titles III and IV. On no reading of the facts is the Article 100 designation the DORA recipient: 0.

The lead-in reads: "Without prejudice to paragraphs 3 and 4, this Regulation applies to the following entities:". It is what turns point (c) into the scope rule: without it, "account information service providers" is only a noun. It is a 2 and not the 3 because it does not name the fintech's category; that element is in point (c). It applies because the need asks whether DORA applies to the fintech; its reservation sends to the exclusions of 2(3) and 2(4), neither of which reaches an AISP.

Scope check: DORA 3(35) takes 'payment institution' from PSD2 4(4), 'a legal person that has been granted authorisation in accordance with Article 11', and DORA 3(36) limits the exempted ones to those 'exempted pursuant to Article 32(1)', which covers only 'payment services as referred to in points (1) to (6) of Annex I'. On the stated facts, a fintech that 'never holds or moves users' money' and 'is registered' is neither, and no reasonable unstated fact makes it one. DORA lists it separately under point (c) and 3(37), so the PSD2 33(2) assimilation raises no real doubt of interpretation. Under 'Twins and repeated wording' this parallel regime is graded 0, not 1: its contrast with the founders' 'licensed payment firms' is not context the answer needs, because the answer (DORA applies through point (c)) does not use it.

Read with the lead-in of 2(1), "this Regulation applies to the following entities: ... account information service providers" answers the primary question directly: DORA applies to AISPs, listed in their own point next to credit institutions (a) and payment institutions (b), with no licence condition, which refutes the founders' assumption. The stated facts establish that the fintech is one: its app, with each user's permission, collects the balances and transactions of the user's accounts at several banks and shows them in one place, an account information service under PSD2 4(16); it never holds or moves money, so it provides only that service; and it is registered rather than authorised, which is the AISP of PSD2 33(1) that DORA 3(37) names. No exclusion of 2(3) or 2(4) reaches an AISP.

"entities referred to in paragraph 1, points (a) to (t), shall collectively be referred to as 'financial entities'". Point (c) is within (a) to (t), so the fintech is a 'financial entity', the addressee of DORA's requirements, unlike the ICT third-party service providers of point (u). Useful context on what applying means, but the yes or no answer comes from 2(1) and point (c), and a complete answer can leave it out.

"This Regulation does not apply to:" managers of alternative investment funds under Article 3(2) of Directive 2011/61/EU, insurance and reinsurance undertakings under Article 4 of Directive 2009/138/EC, IORPs with no more than 15 members, persons exempted under Articles 2 and 3 of Directive 2014/65/EU, SME insurance intermediaries and post office giro institutions. It is the exclusion the lead-in of 2(1) reserves, so an answer may check it, but the facts rule it out: an account information service provider is none of those categories. An exception ruled out by the facts is a 1.

"'account information service provider' means an account information service provider as referred to in Article 33(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/2366". It fixes the meaning of the term in 2(1)(c) and separates it from the categories the founders have in mind: DORA's AISP is the PSD2 33(1) person who provides only the account information service and is registered instead of authorised, not a 'payment institution' (3(35)) nor one exempted under PSD2 32(1) (3(36)). Without it the fintech could be placed under (b) or thought to be outside DORA for lack of a licence. It applies because the fintech only aggregates account information and is registered.

Article 16(1) is a derogation ('Articles 5 to 15 of this Regulation shall not apply to ...'), and the stated facts rule it out. Its tempting category, 'payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366', is limited by DORA 3(36) to those 'exempted pursuant to Article 32(1)'. A registered provider that only collects and shows account data is an account information service provider (DORA 3(37), PSD2 33(1)), and the list does not name that category. Under 'Exceptions, conditions and derogations' a derogation the facts rule out is graded 1, not 0: it shows that no simplified framework replaces Articles 5 to 15 for the fintech, which is context a correct answer to whether DORA applies can leave out.

"The requirements laid down in this Chapter shall also apply to operational or security payment-related incidents ... where they concern credit institutions, payment institutions, account information service providers, and electronic money institutions." It confirms that DORA's incident chapter reaches AISPs, but it extends one chapter to payment-related incidents and presupposes that the entity is in scope; whether DORA applies is decided by 2(1)(c). Context a complete answer can leave out.

"for ... account information service providers as referred to in Article 33(1) of Directive (EU) 2015/2366, the competent authority designated in accordance with Article 22 of Directive (EU) 2015/2366". It names AISPs among the entities whose compliance with DORA a competent authority ensures, the PSD2 authority with which the fintech is registered, and repeats the link to PSD2 33(1). Useful context; applicability itself is settled by 2(1)(c) and 3(37).

Hard negative: "the Commission shall assess ... the appropriateness of extending the scope of this Regulation to operators of payment systems and entities involved in payment-processing activities". It tempts because it suggests that some payment-sector firms sit outside DORA pending a review, which seems to confirm the founders' assumption. It is wrong on the stated facts: it is a review mandate addressed to the Commission that applies to no entity; it concerns operators of payment systems and payment-processing entities, and the fintech, which never holds or moves money, is neither; as an AISP it is already in scope under 2(1)(c).

DORA 2.1.c and 3.37 reach the fintech only if it is an 'account information service provider' under PSD2 33(1), i.e. one 'providing only the payment service as referred to in point (8) of Annex I'; Annex I is not in the corpus, so 4.16 ('an online service to provide consolidated information on one or more payment accounts held ... with more than one payment service provider') is the only text that says what that service is, and it shows that a firm that 'never holds or moves' money still falls in the category, which is the founders' error. Under the definitions rule the node is a 2 because it is needed 'to decide whether a rule applies' and the term 'narrows the scope or separates plausible legal categories' (online service, payment accounts, consolidated information, as against a mere tech provider), so without it the need could reasonably be answered wrongly or incompletely; it is not a 3 because it classifies the activity and does not state the scope rule asked for.

"'account information service provider' means a payment service provider pursuing business activities as referred to in point (8) of Annex I". It is the PSD2 definition of the term DORA uses and links point (8) of Annex I, which the corpus does not hold, to the account information business. For DORA, though, the term is fixed by DORA 3(37) through PSD2 33(1), whose article heading names the account information service providers, and the activity is matched by 4(16); a complete answer can leave this node out.

Under the lead-in "Member States shall establish a public register in which the following are entered:", point (b) reads "natural and legal persons benefiting from an exemption pursuant to Article 32 or 33, and their agents". It explains the stated fact that the fintech is registered with its national supervisor rather than licensed: an AISP exempt under Article 33 is entered in the public register. Context only: DORA's scope does not turn on registration, and the answer does not need this node.

Under the heading 'Account information service providers': "Natural or legal persons providing only the payment service as referred to in point (8) of Annex I shall be exempt from the application of the procedure and conditions set out in Sections 1 and 2, with the exception of ... Articles 14 and 15." It is the provision DORA 3(37) names, so it fixes who is an AISP for DORA: a person providing only the account information service, exempt from authorisation but registered under Articles 14 and 15. Without it 3(37) is circular and the founders' 'licensed' premise cannot be answered. It applies because the fintech only aggregates account information, never holds or moves money, and is registered rather than authorised.

"The persons referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article shall be treated as payment institutions, save that Titles III and IV shall not apply to them ...". Useful context against the founders' assumption, since even PSD2 assimilates an AISP to a payment institution. But it governs the application of PSD2, not DORA's scope, which names AISPs separately in 2(1)(c) and defines them by 33(1) (3(37)); a complete answer can leave it out, and it does not place the fintech under 2(1)(b).
